item.title: El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
item.description:
El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as JeffByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 10:35 AM
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.
Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.
Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”

item.title: A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
item.description:
A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in ThailandByJINTAMAS SAKSORNCHAI Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 10:56 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.
At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.
The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.

item.title: Brazil's Senate approves Lula's $10 billion fiscal package after costly election spending
item.description:
Brazil's Senate approves Lula's $10 billion fiscal package after costly election spending
Brazil’s Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late OctoberByMAURICIO SAVARESE Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 5:56 PM
SAO PAULO -- SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil 's Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October led market analysts to worry about Brazil’s economy. The 81-year-old leader came back with a series of incentives to voters after losing the first round of voting to Flávio Bolsonaro.
The Brazilian government’s fiscal package, which will also have to be approved by the lower house, introduces new rules to slow down the growth of spending, limits corporate tax breaks and closes loopholes. It seeks to improve the ‌public finances by up to 60 billion reais (about $10 billion) next year.
Lula’s move is laying bare the challenges ahead of his fourth nonconsecutive administration, as it already has many critics left and right. Many of his supporters see the plan as a risk to welfare programs, while his critics among market agents deem it to be too shy.
Many analysts say Lula's fiscal package is too dependent on boosting revenues rather than cutting expenses. That perception has led to the depreciation of Brazilian assets in recent days, including the country's real currency. Lula is yet to announce who will be his finance minister for the new term.
Lula’s victories in 2002 and 2022 also sparked immediate depreciation of Brazilian assets, but stock markets eventually recovered from high losses.

item.title: Iran war dents Middle East sports as events are canceled. F1 bucks the trend
item.description:
Iran war dents Middle East sports as events are canceled. F1 bucks the trend
The season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports eventsBySTEPHEN WADE AP sports writerNovember 18, 2026, 12:07 AM
Two season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events. This includes two Formula 1 races earlier this year in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.
The conflict has upended the region's image as a safe haven where governments and sponsors have kicked in billions to lure mega-sports events. This comes as Europe and North America appear wary of such lavish spending.
“The situation could change but the geography will not change,” Sebastian Sons, who follows sports in the Middle East with the German research institute CARPO, told The Associated Press. “The Middle East and the Gulf region are always a volatile and fragile region.”
Going ahead is an endorsement for doing business in the region, but has also prompted concerns about safety from some teams and staff. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of auto racing's world governing body FIA, has said “we are fully prepared” to pull off the two races: Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.
Ben Sulayem is from the United Arab Emirates.
A MotoGP race was held in Qatar on Nov. 8 on the track where F1 races. MotoGP is operated by Liberty Media, which also runs F1.
“Holding the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi signals that those two are stable and able to host large-scale sporting events. It is important they are seen to be open for business,” Kristian Ulrichsen, a political scientist at Rice University's Baker Institute, told The AP.

item.title: St. Peter's Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of Roman Catholicism
item.description:
St. Peter's Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of Roman Catholicism
St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedicationByTRISHA THOMAS Associated Press and COLLEEN BARRY Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 11:13 AM
Share
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism whose commanding dome defines the Roman skyline, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication Wednesday, a monument to artistic achievement and perseverance.
Its construction spanned 120 years, 20 pontificates and the work of a succession of 12 architects, enduring the Protestant Reformation and the sack of Rome before Pope Urban VIII dedicated it on Nov. 18, 1626.
“You walk through those doors and you won’t feel the conflicts and the disasters and the setbacks,” said Elizabeth Lev, a Rome-based American art historian. “You walk through those doors and you see continuity and beauty and achievement and triumph.”
A setting for papal ceremonies and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year, the basilica was built over the traditional burial site of the Apostle Peter, replacing a church that had stood for more than a millennium.
Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone on April 18, 1506, launching a project whose architects included Donato Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, who completed its facade.
Even on the day of its dedication, the basilica’s familiar setting was still taking shape.
“The church facade was complete, but the amazing piazza, which is part and parcel of the church we know today, wasn’t there yet,” Lev said.
“As a matter of fact, you would have heard lots of people complaining about the new facade and how it blocked Michelangelo’s dome,” she said.

item.title: Ukraine criticizes IAEA plan to appoint sanctioned Russian official to senior post
item.description:
Ukraine criticizes IAEA plan to appoint sanctioned Russian official to senior post
Ukraine has criticized the proposal by the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official, sanctioned by Kyiv, to a senior positionBySTEPHANIE LIECHTENSTEIN Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 11:13 AM
Share
VIENNA -- VIENNA (AP) — Ukraine on Wednesday denounced a proposal by the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official sanctioned by Kyiv to a senior position at the U.N. nuclear watchdog in Vienna.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the proposed appointment of Alexey Ferapontov as deputy director general “categorically unacceptable” and urged IAEA chief Rafael Mariano Grossi to “abandon this appointment" in a post on X.
In a note sent Nov. 16 to all 35 members of the IAEA Board of Governors, which was seen by The Associated Press, Grossi proposed the nomination of Ferapontov to the position of deputy director general in the Department of Nuclear Energy.
The note also proposed a candidate from the United States to the position of deputy director general in the Department of Management, and a candidate from North Macedonia to become director in the Department of Safeguards.
Grossi suggested holding an informal briefing about the senior appointments with members of the board this week. According to the IAEA’s Statute and staff regulations, the IAEA director general has the authority to appoint staff members.
“Ferapontov is subject to Ukrainian sanctions for his involvement in Russia’s attempts to legitimize the illegal seizure of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant,” Sybiha wrote on X. “Officials implicated in such violations should face accountability, not be rewarded with senior positions in international organizations,” he added.

item.title: The UK and EU are holding a summit to patch up ties after their bitter Brexit divorce
item.description:
The UK and EU are holding a summit to patch up ties after their bitter Brexit divorce
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is meeting EU officials in Brussels on Friday to discuss closer ties between the UK and the bloc that it left in 2020ByJILL LAWLESS Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 2:02 PM
LONDON -- Britain and the European Union went through a bitter divorce, then slowly tried to be friends again.
Now they are starting to consider maybe, one day, getting back together.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet the EU’s top officials in Brussels on Friday for a summit that the British leader has called a step toward undoing a decade of damage triggered by the U.K.'s 2016 vote to leave the bloc.
“The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained,” Burnham said this week. He has said that all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc.
Burnham has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and is far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but of a mistrustful EU.
Still, Burnham has broken British governments’ decade-long code of silence on the option of rejoining.
Most economists agree that Brexit has hurt the British economy by erecting barriers to trade with the country's neighbors, but U.K. politicians have been wary of reopening a painful debate. Both sides of the argument remember the anger and divisiveness of the referendum campaign and the acrimonious divorce negotiations that followed before the final split in 2020.
Friday’s EU-U.K. summit is only the second since Britain became the first country ever to leave the world’s biggest trading bloc. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on social media that she wanted it to be “a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security.”

item.title: Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails weapons produced in the country
item.description:
Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails weapons produced in the country
Ukraine says it has carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern RussiaByHANNA ARHIROVA Associated Press and BARRY HATTON Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 10:09 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia, officials said Wednesday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the effectiveness of Kyiv’s domestically produced weapons that damaged the key Kerch Bridge between Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Attacks by both sides have continued even as delegations await word on another round of U.S.-mediated talks. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to discuss the nearly five-year war with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia on Thursday during a visit to China.
Ukraine’s General Staff said that storage tanks were hit at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit was struck at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, which were also targeted on Sunday night, can process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the front line in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.
Russian officials reported attacks on two industrial enterprises in the region, but they gave no details.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted refineries as Ukraine seeks to hurt Russia’s oil sector, a mainstay of its economy, and Moscow presses on with its all-out invasion of its neighbor.
“Our technologies and companies are developing very well,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.
Ukraine's cutting-edge long-range drones and missiles were deployed against the Kerch Bridge in a large-scale attack on Monday night that was prepared over weeks, he said.
“Right now, we’re in the top three in the world for tech development. In Europe, I think we’re number one,” Zelenskyy said.

item.title: Mexico's Catholic street DJs turn annual pilgrimage into a party
item.description:
Mexico's Catholic street DJs turn annual pilgrimage into a party
A mix of street DJs and Catholic devotees are taking to the streets in one of Mexico's most important pilgrimagesByMARTÍN SILVA REY Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 4:22 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MEXICO CITY -- A sea of people carrying statues of Mexico's patron saint, the Virgin of Guadalupe, marched along the avenue leading up to the country's most important basilica on Wednesday.
Such pilgrimages are practically embedded in the daily rhythms of the bustling Mexican capital. But the roughly 1,000 pilgrims from across the Latin American nation aren't just Catholic devotees.
They're also Mexican street DJs.
The annual procession and street party known as the “sonidero” pilgrimage is perhaps one of the most Mexico City-esque convergences of celebrations to hit the city.
Sonideros, as they're known, are a particular brand of DJs found primarily in Mexico City, but also in other parts of Mexico and Colombia. The DJs mix rhythmic tunes of cumbia with radio announcements, chanting shout outs that mingle with the music.
The tradition is so important in the city, particularly in working-class neighborhoods, that in 2023 the city government recognized sonidero culture as intangible cultural heritage — a designation UNESCO quickly celebrated. The music has even evolved into its own dance, a derivation of cumbia that has more open steps meant for street parties than the classic two-person cumbia.
Each neighborhood has its own set of sonideros who organize pop-up mobile parties. Wednesday's party-procession on the avenue leading up to the famed Basilica de Guadalupe wasn't so spontaneous, but rather part of an annual celebration now spanning decades.
“The root of faith in Mexico is the Virgin of Guadalupe,” said Christian Castañeda, a musician who joined the throngs of people marching through the gates of the Basilica. “We mix this party with the joy of music...

item.title: Migrants face severe health tolls amid South Africa's anti-illegal migration tensions
item.description:
Migrants face severe health tolls amid South Africa's anti-illegal migration tensions
Aid groups in South Africa report that anti-illegal migration protests have severely impacted the health of migrantsByMOGOMOTSI MAGOME Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 9:11 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
JOHANNESBURG -- Migrants affected by protests against illegal immigration in South Africa have suffered devastating impacts to their health as they avoided visiting medical facilities or left the country to avoid violence in recent months, aid groups said Wednesday.
Many migrants who had been receiving medication in South Africa for HIV, tuberculosis and other ailments have had their treatment severely disrupted, they said.
Children, pregnant women and people traveling with newborns have been among the most affected, while others suffered physical injuries and illnesses including respiratory infections, high blood pressure and gastrointestinal issues during rushed journeys home from South Africa, they said.
South Africa has been gripped by anti-illegal migration protests accusing foreigners in the country illegally of committing crimes, stealing jobs amid high unemployment and overburdening public services. Tens of thousands have voluntarily repatriated to their home countries including Malawi, Nigeria and Ghana. Some fled after violent attacks.
Some protesters have blocked foreigners from accessing clinics and other public health facilities, claiming they are exclusively reserved for South Africans even though the law allows foreigners to receive treatment there.
“Many migrants at displacement sites reported not accessing healthcare for many months, and up to a year in some cases, due to fear of being turned away or harmed," said Claire Waterhouse, the Doctors Without Borders advocacy director for Southern Africa.
